strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior procedural-text work focuses on action sequences, while business rules with inter-rule logical dependencies (sequential, conditional, parallel) are largely unexplored; the <Condition, Action> formalization with logical-judgment attributes is well motivated.

The BPRF dataset construction follows a careful, documented pipeline (LLM-assisted and web collection, three annotators, independent verification by three further experts), with reasonable quality controls reported (ICC 0.904 for text quality, Fleiss' Kappa 0.911 after BIO reformulation).

Comprehensive evaluation covering 12 LLMs (closed- and open-source, including reasoning-oriented models) across 5 prompt variants and 3 tasks (rule extraction as NER, logical-judgment classification, dependency classification), with prompts and templates detailed in the appendix.
The case study comparing DeepSeek v3 vs. DeepSeek r1 with the model's reasoning trace is illustrative and supports the claim that reasoning-oriented models better capture nested dependencies.
The paper is clearly written, with formal definitions, examples (Tables 1, 7-9), and figures that make the annotation schema and framework easy to follow.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is very small: 50 texts and 326 rules (with dependency labels split 157/24/33 across sequential/conditional/parallel), which limits statistical power, the reliability of macro-averaged F1 comparisons, and generalizability; no statistical significance tests are reported for any model or prompt comparison.

A substantial and unspecified portion of the data is synthetically generated by ChatGPT 3.5; the ratio of synthetic to real texts is not reported, and contamination/similarity between synthetic data and the knowledge of the evaluated LLMs is not discussed, raising questions about what the benchmark actually measures.

Metric reporting is inconsistent: in Table 6 some models are compared on 'Macro F1' (e.g., DeepSeek r1 0.7542, QwQ-32b 0.7161) while others (GPT o1 0.7118) appear to be compared on accuracy, making cross-model claims unreliable; per-class results and confusion matrices are absent despite severe class imbalance.

The dependency-classification stage is evaluated on gold rule pairs, but the interaction between extraction errors and dependency errors (end-to-end pipeline evaluation) is not measured, so the reported numbers do not reflect deployable performance.

The ExIde framework is essentially a set of five prompt variants; there is limited technical novelty, no non-prompting baselines (e.g., fine-tuned encoders or prior frameworks such as Bellan et al. 2022), and ablations of prompt components are only interpreted anecdotally.

Several analysis claims rest on single examples (one flight-booking case for NER, one deposit case for logical judgment, one shopping case for dependency), which is thin evidence for the qualitative conclusions drawn.

Dataset release is only promised upon acceptance, and no code or evaluation scripts are provided, weakening reproducibility at review time; annotator expertise and adjudication procedure for disagreements are not described.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: rule-centric business process modeling (condition-action rules with sequential/conditional/parallel dependencies), which is a meaningful departure from action-sequence procedural extraction and relevant to process automation and NLP for procedural text.

The dataset construction process is described with reasonable care: multiple annotators, a separate verification team, transformation to BIO/NER format to enable standard agreement measures, and reported agreement statistics (ICC 0.904, Fleiss' Kappa 0.911).

The evaluation covers a reasonably broad and current set of 12 LLMs (including reasoning-oriented models like GPT o1, DeepSeek r1, QwQ-32b) and 5 prompt variants, and the analysis of reasoning traces (Fig. 15) offers some qualitative insight into why reasoning models do better on dependency classification.
The Limitations section is candid about dataset size, synthetic data, prompt sensitivity, and pairwise-only dependency modeling.
weaknesses: The dataset is very small (50 texts, 326 rules, only 214 dependency-labeled pairs) and a substantial, unspecified portion is synthetically generated by ChatGPT 3.5. This creates both a distributional-bias problem and a potential circularity concern: LLM-generated templated text is used to evaluate LLMs, likely inflating NER F1 scores (~0.9) relative to naturally occurring business documents.

The class distribution for Logical Judgement is extremely skewed (205 'contains' vs. 1 'less than' and 1 'greater than or equal to'), making Macro-F1 on this task statistically unreliable and the reported rankings (e.g., QwQ-32b at 0.6397) difficult to interpret. No significance testing, variance estimates, or multiple-run protocol is reported anywhere.

The methodological contribution (ExIde) is limited to prompt engineering with a shared template and minor variations (e.g., Prompt 3 merely renames the input field). There are no non-LLM baselines, no fine-tuning comparison, and no comparison to prior procedural-extraction systems, so the empirical claims about the framework's effectiveness are weakly supported.

Reproducibility is a concern: the dataset is only promised 'upon acceptance', no code or prompts-in-code release is stated, and key experimental details (decoding parameters, number of runs, how rule pairs are constructed for the dependency task, whether dependency classification is evaluated on gold or extracted rules) are missing or ambiguous.

The annotation and evaluation design has inconsistencies: three annotators rate synthetic text quality, but the ratio of real vs. synthetic documents is never disclosed; the 'verification' stage's disagreement-resolution procedure is not described; and it is unclear whether annotators are true domain experts or NLP students.

The case study on dependency classification is anecdotal (a single shopping scenario with 10 pairs), yet it is used to support fairly strong claims about reasoning models. The related-work positioning acknowledges a prior 'linear process flows' work by the same authors but the delta is not sharply justified.

Writing and presentation are uneven: several figures are low-resolution screenshots of chat-style prompts, tables mix accuracy and Macro-F1 without justification, and the paper reads in places as a system report rather than an analysis with testable hypotheses.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior procedural-text work focuses on action sequences, while rule flows (condition-action pairs with sequential/conditional/parallel dependencies) capture decision logic that existing datasets like PAGED do not represent. The framing of 'rule-based vs. action-based' process modeling is well motivated.

The BPRF dataset construction follows a reasonable protocol: collection from real domains plus synthetic generation, annotation by three domain experts, verification by three additional experts, and quantitative quality checks (ICC 0.904 on text quality, Fleiss' Kappa 0.911 on BIO tags), which exceeds the reporting standard of many resource papers.

The evaluation is broad in coverage: 12 LLMs (5 closed-source, 7 open-source, including reasoning-focused models) across 5 prompt variants, with separate metrics for the NER-style extraction task, logical judgement classification, and dependency classification.

The qualitative case study comparing DeepSeek v3 and DeepSeek r1, including inspection of the reasoning trace (Fig. 15), adds interpretive value and concretely illustrates why reasoning-oriented models handle nested/parallel dependencies better.
The limitations section is candid and accurate: dataset size, synthetic-data bias, prompt sensitivity, and the pairwise-only dependency model are all acknowledged.
weaknesses: The dataset is small (50 documents, 326 rules, 258 sentences), and a substantial portion is synthetically generated by ChatGPT 3.5. Evaluating LLMs on LLM-generated business texts raises circularity concerns (models may handle GPT-generated text unusually well), and the paper does not report the real-vs-synthetic split or per-source results. The near-ceiling NER scores (~0.92-0.93 for most models) suggest the extraction benchmark is not very discriminative.

The methodology is prompt-engineering only. There are no fine-tuned baselines, no comparison against existing procedural/process extraction systems (e.g., the cited Ren et al. 2023b or LM-GNN approaches adapted to this setting), so the 'framework' contribution reduces to a set of prompt variants and it is unclear how it compares to non-LLM alternatives.

Several evaluation-design details are underspecified: it is unclear whether dependency classification is performed on gold rule pairs or on extracted rules (error propagation between the two stages is not measured); the pairwise construction for dependency labels and how 'no relationship' pairs are sampled is not described; no significance testing or variance estimates accompany the score comparisons, several of which are very small (e.g., 0.928 vs. 0.934).

The dependency labels are heavily imbalanced (157 sequential / 24 conditional / 33 parallel) and Macro-F1 alone, without per-class breakdowns or confusion matrices, hides whether the conditional class—the most interesting one—is learned at all.

Some reporting is inconsistent or confusing: bolded values in Tables 4-6 do not always correspond to the best scores; 'accuracy' and 'Macro-F1' are used interchangeably for dependency classification without definition; the claim that Prompt 1 achieves 'an average NER score of 1.0' on one example is anecdotal and not placed in a quantitative error analysis.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the dataset is promised only 'upon paper acceptance', and no code repository, decoding parameters (temperature, seeds), or number of runs is reported, despite the authors' own acknowledgment of prompt/formatting sensitivity.

The prompt-variant analysis yields only weak, post-hoc qualitative explanations for why Implicit Mapping wins on NER but Logical Judgement wins on classification; the contribution of the five variants to understanding is limited given the small deltas.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem—the extraction of condition–action rules and their logical dependencies (Sequential, Conditional, Parallel) from regulatory/business text—providing a clear motivation ('Logic Gap') and a well-differentiated position against prior action-centric procedural-text benchmarks (Table 6 comparison is helpful).

The BREX benchmark construction pipeline is carefully described: expert annotation by three annotators, independent multi-stage verification by another three experts, and quantitative quality checks (ICC 0.892 for text quality; Fleiss' Kappa 0.901 via a reasonable NER-projection proxy for structured-annotation agreement).

The empirical study is broad: 13 LLMs across 5 families (closed- and open-source, instruction-tuned and reasoning-optimized), 5 prompting strategies sharing the same output schema (a controlled design), and two evaluation stages (rule extraction and dependency identification).

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: robustness under rule density and reasoning complexity, a documented failure mode of P4 (over-merging enumerated values under equal), a documented failure mode of P5 (reification of discourse-level connectors into spurious meta-rules), with concrete case studies in the appendix.

Prompt templates (Figs. 10–15), the synthetic-data generation prompt (Fig. 9), annotation definitions, evaluation dimension definitions, and dataset statistics (Table 5) are all provided, supporting reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
The Limitations and Ethical Statements are substantive and honest (synthetic data usage, quadratic pairwise complexity, restricted logical formalization, downstream misuse).
weaknesses: The central claim that executable grounding (P5) 'significantly outperforms standard prompts' is weakly supported by the reported numbers: the average NER F1 gap between P5 (0.882) and P1/P2 (0.879) is 0.3 points, and P5 is not best for every model (e.g., GPT-5, Kimi-k2-Instruct favor other prompts). No statistical significance testing or variance over runs is reported, so 'significantly' is overstated for Table 2/3; the reasoning-model gap in Table 4 is larger and more convincing.

The contribution of ExIde as a 'framework' is essentially a set of five prompts plus pairwise dependency classification; there are no non-prompting baselines (e.g., fine-tuned models, structured parsers, process-mining approaches), making it hard to gauge whether prompt engineering is the right lens or how far current LLMs are from practical utility (Stage II F1 of 0.42–0.76 suggests substantial headroom).

The dataset is modest in scale (409 documents, 2,855 rules, ~7 rules/doc, only 234 tokens/doc on average), and the proportion of synthetic data is never quantified ('a limited amount'), leaving unclear how representative the high-complexity structures are; contamination risk of benchmark texts (publicly available documents) into the evaluated LLMs is not discussed.

Inter-annotator agreement is only measured on a proxy NER projection (spans for Slot Type, Reference Value, Action) over a subset; agreement on the dependency-graph structure—the paper's core novel annotation—remains unvalidated, and evaluation of model outputs likewise uses string-based tuple matching whose sensitivity to surface-form variation is acknowledged but not systematically addressed (e.g., no semantic matching alternative reported).

It is ambiguous whether Stage II dependency identification operates on gold rules or on model-extracted rules (error propagation between stages is not analyzed), and Figure 3/4 aggregate models into two groups without per-model detail or significance quantification.

Polish issues: the code/dataset availability URL is missing in the text ('available at:' is blank), several typos and awkward phrasings, references with '1 others', and the radar plot in Fig. 3 is hard to read; the title's pun ('Rulesual') may not travel well.

Broader impact on the field is moderate: the benchmark is useful for the specific sub-community (process/business-rule extraction), but the schema's restricted operator set and small size limit its utility as a general logic-awareness benchmark.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: extracting condition–action business rules and their logical dependencies (Sequential/Conditional/Parallel) from regulatory documents, which is a meaningful shift from action-centric procedural text benchmarks.

The benchmark construction pipeline is documented with multi-stage expert verification (three annotators plus three reviewers), and quality control is quantified (ICC 0.892 for text quality; Fleiss' Kappa 0.901 via an NER-projection proxy for structured rules), with a thoughtful justification for why standard IAA metrics do not directly apply to graph-structured annotations.

The evaluation covers 13 LLMs across 5 model families (closed- and open-source), and the analysis goes beyond headline numbers: complexity/density robustness analysis (Fig. 4) and detailed case studies (Appendix A.7) that honestly identify failure modes of both P4 (over-merging enumerated values) and P5 (reification of discourse-level connectors into spurious slots).

Limitations and ethical statements are substantive rather than perfunctory, covering synthetic data usage, quadratic scalability of pairwise dependency modeling, and the limited expressiveness of the dependency schema.
weaknesses: The headline claim that executable grounding (P5) 'significantly outperforms' standard prompting is not supported by the evidence: the average NER F1 gap between P5 (0.882) and P1/P2 (0.879) is about 0.3 points, and per-model results are mixed (e.g., Gemini-2.5-flash and GPT-5 do best with P4 or P1). No statistical significance tests, variance estimates, or multiple-run analyses are reported, so the central claim is within plausible noise.

The baselines are weak and internal: P1–P5 are all variants of the authors' own prompt template, and there is no comparison to any external method (e.g., prior process-extraction or instruction-tuned approaches like Pyrih et al. 2025), supervised fine-tuning, or even a zero-shot prompt without the reasoning format. Claims of 'out-of-the-box solutions for business customers' rest only on this internal prompt comparison.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified in ways that threaten reproducibility: it is unclear how extracted rules are matched to gold rules for NER F1 (exact vs. fuzzy span matching, normalization of actions), how dependency F1 is computed given that it requires first matching predicted rules to gold nodes, how the None class is handled, and how documents are split. The repository link in the abstract is literally empty ('available at:').

There appear to be annotation errors in the released gold data: in Table 10, the ground-truth rule ⟨Monthly deposit amount, >, 200,000⟩ does not match the input text, which states that a single deposit exceeding 200,000 yuan (not the monthly deposit amount) requires proof of source of funds. This undermines confidence in gold-standard quality and suggests the examples should be re-checked.

The dataset is small (409 documents, ~7 rules/document, ~234 tokens/document) and the fraction of synthetic data is never quantified ('a limited amount'), despite synthetic augmentation of exactly the non-linear structures (nested conditions, parallel constraints) that motivate the paper; a leakage-adjacent concern is that the Gemini-2.5 family was used both to generate synthetic documents and as an evaluated model.

The rule schema (Slot Type / Logical Operator / Reference Value + Action) is essentially a task-oriented dialogue slot schema rather than a general business-rule formalism; complex real regulations with temporal constraints, exceptions, and quantification are excluded, and the paper's framing of this as solving the 'Logic Gap' overstates the scope of what is modeled.

The reasoning-optimized vs. instruction-tuned comparison (Section 5.3) is confounded: the model pairs differ in more than 'reasoning mode' (training data, size, version), and with a single run per configuration the +6.0% claim for Qwen3-30B cannot be distinguished from sampling variance.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: the title pun, several awkward phrasings, figures whose axes are mislabeled (Fig. 4 left panels both say 'Rule Count' for what should be logic complexity), and key details (dataset splits, metric computation) relegated to or missing from the appendix entirely.

strengths: BREX addresses a genuine gap: existing procedural-text benchmarks (recipes, tutorials, BPM texts) model action flows, while business regulations require condition–action rules with Sequential/Conditional/Parallel dependencies. The Rule-Flow vs. Action-Flow framing is well motivated and the benchmark comparison table (Table 6) clearly positions the contribution.

The annotation schema is clearly formalized (atomic ⟨Slot Type, Operator, Reference Value, Action⟩ tuples with three dependency types), and multi-stage verification (annotation team + separate review team) plus quality reporting (ICC 0.892 for text quality, Fleiss' Kappa 0.901 via a NER-projection proxy) show reasonable care toward annotation reliability.

The empirical study is broad: five prompting strategies across 13 LLMs (5 families, closed and open source), with analysis along rule density and reasoning-complexity dimensions, and the appendix case studies (Tables 8–10) give concrete, well-diagnosed failure modes (over-merging under 'equal'; P5's reification of discourse-level connectors) that add real analytic value.
The paper is candid about limitations (synthetic augmentation, quadratic pairwise dependency modeling, restricted logical formalization) and includes a substantive ethical statement.
The finding that reasoning-optimized models degrade more gracefully under high reasoning complexity (Figure 4, Table 4) is a plausible and useful empirical observation for logic-intensive extraction.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the abstract states 'The code and dataset are available at:' but the URL is missing from the manuscript. For a benchmark paper, the released resource is the central contribution and its absence is a serious concern for the ARR reproducibility criteria.

The role of synthetic data is under-specified. The paper claims BREX is largely real-world but never quantifies how many of the 409 documents or 2,855 rules are Gemini-generated. This matters both for the 'real-world benchmark' claim and for potential contamination-style biases (the schema used to generate synthetic text embeds the exact annotation conventions, which may make synthetic portions artificially easy).

Inter-annotator agreement is only measured via a NER-projection proxy on a subset, and only for span components. The dependency relations (Sequential/Conditional/Parallel) — the core novelty of the benchmark — have no direct IAA measurement. Given the inherent ambiguity between Sequential and Conditional relations illustrated in Appendix A.2, the reliability of the edge annotations remains unverified.

The headline claim that executable grounding (P5) 'significantly outperforms' standard prompts is not well supported. Table 2 shows P5 at 0.882 vs. P1/P2 at 0.879 — a ~0.3 point average difference, with P5 actually losing to P1 on several models (e.g., GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-flash, Qwen3-235B). No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance is reported anywhere. The +6.0% improvement claim rests on a single model pair (Qwen3-30B).

Key evaluation details are missing: how are predicted rules matched to gold rules for NER F1 (exact tuple matching? alignment algorithm?); and crucially, whether Stage II dependency classification is evaluated over gold rule pairs (oracle extraction) or over the model's own Stage I predictions. This ambiguity makes Table 4 hard to interpret and the framework hard to reproduce.

Documents average only 234 tokens and 7 rules, and NER F1 for top models is ~0.89–0.91, suggesting the extraction portion of the benchmark may be near saturation and simpler than the framing suggests; the interesting difficulty is concentrated in Stage II, where absolute F1 (~0.43–0.76) is low and setup clarity matters most.

No fine-tuned baselines are included despite the paper's own argument that fine-tuning is often impractical; a small fine-tuned model (or prior process-extraction systems) would strengthen claims that prompting-level interventions are the right comparison point. The five prompts also confound several changes at once (P3 is a near-trivial input relabeling), weakening the 'systematic' ablation framing.

The claimed '30+ vertical domains' coverage is not substantiated: no domain distribution table is provided, and all examples and case studies come from banking/service scenarios, raising doubt about actual breadth and balance.

Writing and presentation issues: Figures 3–4 lack readable axis calibration in places; the radar plot has no numeric support in the text; and the missing dataset link (also affecting the title typo 'Rulesual' aside) should be fixed before camera-ready.
